eurotrochilus:enwiki:10.title: Eurotrochilus (Co-evolution of ornithophilous flowers and extinction)

facts.statement: The genus Eurotrochilus was described by Gerald Mayr in 2004.
facts.quote: authority: Mayr, 2004

facts.statement: Two species are currently recognized: E. inexpectatus described by Mayr in 2004 and E. noniewiczi described by Bochenski in 2007.
facts.quote: subdivision: E. inexpectatus Mayr, 2004 E. noniewiczi Bochenski, 2007

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus lived during the Rupelian age of the Early Oligocene epoch within the Paleogene period.
facts.quote: Eurotrochilus has been dated back to the Rupelian age of the early Oligocene era, which occurred during the Paleogene period.

facts.statement: Recent estimates suggest Eurotrochilus lived between 28 and 34 million years ago, though the exact timing is debated.
facts.quote: While there is some debate over exactly when Eurotrochilus was present, the most recent estimate is suggested to be 28 to 34 million years ago.

facts.statement: Fossils found in Germany, France, and Poland indicate that the Old World was the origin of the hummingbird family, despite all living species today being found in the New World.
facts.quote: The discovery of Eurotrochilus fossils in Germany, France, and Poland was extremely important because today all 328 of the extant species of hummingbirds only occur in the New World but the fossils of Eurotrochilus suggest an Old World origin.

facts.statement: Although morphologically similar to modern hummingbirds, Eurotrochilus retained primitive features and is not closely related to any specific living species.
facts.quote: Despite Eurotrochilus being morphologically very similar to modern hummingbirds, they still retained several primitive features and are not closely related to any specific extant hummingbird in the crown group.

facts.statement: The species E. noniewiczi is named after Edward Noniewicza, the private collector who discovered the fossil specimen.
facts.quote: The name of the second species, E. noniewiczi, refers to the surname of the private collector, Edward Noniewicza, who found the fossil specimen.

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus is an extinct genus of stem-group hummingbirds and represents the closest known relatives to the crown group Trochilidae.
facts.quote: Eurotrochilus is an extinct genus of stem group hummingbirds (Trochilidae) and are the closest known relatives of the crown group Trochilidae.

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus specimens are among the smallest fossil birds and are classified in the order Apodiformes due to their shortened humeri and ulnae.
facts.quote: Eurotrochilus specimens are some of the smallest fossil birds and are referred to the order Apodiformes due to their strongly abbreviated humeri and ulnae.

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus possessed elongated beaks, a feature unknown in Jungornis, which serves as evidence of their ability to consume nectar.
facts.quote: Another difference is that Eurotrochilus have elongated beaks (unknown in Jungornis), which is evidence of nectarivory, the ability to consume nectar from flowers.

facts.statement: In some species, the skull and beak of Eurotrochilus have been measured to be approximately 34 millimeters in length.
facts.quote: In some species of Eurotrochilus, the skull and beak have been roughly measured to be 34 millimeters.

facts.statement: The beaks of Eurotrochilus are straight and narrow, measuring 15.5 to 20 millimeters in length, which is roughly 2.5 times the length of the cranium.
facts.quote: The beaks of Eurotrochilus are greatly elongated, straight, and narrow, measuring from 15.5 to 20 millimeters in length, roughly 2.5 times as long as the cranium.

facts.statement: The widely separated maxillary processes in the palatine bones indicate that Eurotrochilus possessed rhynchokinesis, the ability to flex the upper beak.
facts.quote: The maxillary processes of the palatine bones in the beaks of Eurotrochilus are widely separated, indicating the presence of rhynchokinesis, or the ability to flex the upper beak.

facts.statement: Large hyoid bones in Eurotrochilus are thought to have supported a long, protractile tongue used for lapping up nectar.
facts.quote: The large hyoid bones are thought to support a long protractile tongue, which extant hummingbirds use to lap up nectar.

facts.statement: Adaptations in Eurotrochilus allowed it to consume nectar from ornithophilous flowers as its main nutrient source and to pollinate those flowers.
facts.quote: All of these adaptations made it possible for Eurotrochilus to consume nectar from ornithophilous flowers, its main source of nutrients, and to pollinate these flowers as well.

facts.statement: The ulna of Eurotrochilus measures between 6.7 and 8.8 millimeters, which is shorter than the 13-millimeter ulna found in Jungornis.
facts.quote: The ulna of Eurotrochilus measures between 6.7 and 8.8 millimeters, which is shorter than the ulna of Jungornis, which measures 13 millimeters.

facts.statement: The humeri of Eurotrochilus measure between 6.0 and 6.5 millimeters and are considered short and stout compared to other Apodiformes, except extant hummingbirds.
facts.quote: The humeri of Eurotrochilus have been measured to be between 6.0 and 6.5 millimeters. It is considered short and stout when compared to other Apodiformes, except extant hummingbirds.

facts.statement: Specializations in the humeri of Eurotrochilus allowed the bone to rotate during hovering flight.
facts.quote: These morphological specializations of the humeri allow the bone to rotate during hovering flight.

facts.statement: It is debated exactly when Eurotrochilus was present, with recent estimates suggesting a range of 28 to 34 million years ago.
facts.quote: While there is some debate over exactly when Eurotrochilus was present, the most recent estimate is suggested to be 28 to 34 million years ago.

facts.statement: Dr. Gerald Mayr first described the extinct bird Eurotrochilus in 2004 after finding tiny skeletons in museum drawers.
facts.quote: Eurotrochilus was first described by Dr. Gerald Mayr in 2004 when he found two previously unidentified tiny bird skeletons in the drawers of the Stuttgart National History Museum.

facts.statement: Six specimens of Eurotrochilus have been found across Germany, France, and Poland.
facts.quote: Six Eurotrochilus specimens have been identified in three countries of central Europe: Germany, France, and Poland.

facts.statement: Two distinct species of Eurotrochilus have been identified: E. inexpectatus and E. noniewiczi.
facts.quote: Two species have been identified, E. inexpectatus and E. noniewiczi.

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus provided the strongest evidence that modern-looking hummingbirds existed in the Old World during the early Oligocene.
facts.quote: The discovery of the fossil hummingbird Eurotrochilus inexpectatus was a significant discovery because it provided the most convincing evidence for the presence of modern-looking hummingbirds of stem-group Trochilidae in the Old World.

facts.statement: Dr. Antoine Louchart described a French specimen of Eurotrochilus in 2007, which included an almost complete skeleton preserved on a slab.
facts.quote: In 2007, Dr. Antoine Louchart described a specimen found in the Le Grand Banc Strata in southeastern France that consisted of an almost complete skeleton on a slab.

facts.statement: The Polish specimen found at Winnica serves as the holotype for the new species Eurotrochilus noniewiczi.
facts.quote: The specimen is the holotype for a new species of Eurotrochilus, E. noniewiczi.

facts.statement: Harald and Annette Oechsler discovered a fourth specimen of E. inexpectatus in 2009 at a clay pit in Southern Germany.
facts.quote: In 2009, Harald and Annette Oechsler found the fourth specimen of Eurotrochilus inexpectatus in the former clay pit of the Bott-Eder GmbH ("Grube Unterfeld") in Wiesloch-Frauenweiler of Southern Germany.

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus lived during the Rupelian age of the early Oligocene era.
facts.quote: The paleoenvironment of Eurotrochilus species occurred during the Rupelian age of the early Oligocene era.

facts.statement: Specimens of Eurotrochilus date to between 28 and 34 million years ago, with German fossils estimated at 32 million years old.
facts.quote: German specimens are estimated to be 32 million years old, the French specimen is estimated to be 28-34 million years old, and Polish specimens are estimated to be 31 million years old.

facts.statement: During the Oligocene, the Paratethys Ocean covered most of Central and Eastern Europe where Eurotrochilus fossils were found.
facts.quote: During the Oligocene era, the Paratethys Ocean covered the majority of Central and Eastern Europe.

facts.statement: The Polish site where E. noniewiczi was discovered was once submerged under the Paratethys Ocean.
facts.quote: The Winnica site in Poland where the E. noniewiczi specimen was found used to be submerged in the Paratethys Ocean.

facts.statement: Fossils found alongside Eurotrochilus suggest the local climate was sub-tropical to tropical.
facts.quote: Based on the other species found alongside all the Eurotrochilus specimens, the local climate is believed to have been sub-tropical to tropical.

facts.statement: The warm climate supported broad-leaved evergreen forests and palm-rich coastal forests where Eurotrochilus lived.
facts.quote: The warm, frost-free climate would have supported broad-leaved evergreen forests as well as palm-rich coastal forests on sandy soils.

facts.statement: Scientists believe Eurotrochilus experienced mild winters based on its fruit and nectar diet, though migration habits are unknown.
facts.quote: It is difficult to estimate the winter conditions during this period without knowing the migratory habits of the avian species but based on their fruit and nectar diets, scientists believe that this area of Europe most likely experienced mild winters.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Old World bird-pollinated flowers evolved their specific shapes in response to Eurotrochilus, which had long beaks, tongues, and hovering flight.
facts.quote: Considering that Eurotrochilus had long beaks and tongues to consume nectar as well as the ability to hover while in flight, it seems plausible to conclude that ornithophilous flowers in the Old World evolved bird-pollination morphologies in response to Eurotrochilus.

facts.statement: The abundance of E. inexpectatus fossils suggests these birds were locally dominant pollinators of ornithophilous flowers in the early Oligocene.
facts.quote: The abundance of E. inexpectatus specimens at the Frauenweiler site in Southern Germany suggests that Eurotrochilus were possibly locally abundant during the early Oligocene, making them the most likely dominant pollinators of ornithophilous flowers.

facts.statement: It is debated whether competition with long-tongued bees caused the extinction of Eurotrochilus and European hummingbirds.
facts.quote: Ecological competition with long-tongued bees for ornithophilous flowers is a suggested explanation for the extinction of Eurotrochilus and modern hummingbirds in Europe.

facts.statement: Rapid climate change is another hypothesis for the extinction of Eurotrochilus, which would have been difficult for such a small bird to survive.
facts.quote: Another possible explanation for their extinction is rapid climate change from the suspected moderate tropical climate, which would have been a critical problem considering the small size of Eurotrochilus.

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus belongs to the family Trochilidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Trochilidae

facts.statement: Eurotrochilus lived between 33.9 and 27.3 million years ago during the Rupelian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Rupelian (33.9 to 27.3 million years ago)

rejected.quote: The specific epithet of E. inexpectatus is Latin for 'unexpected', indicative of the surprise felt by Gerald Mayr and his team when they discovered a modern-type fossil hummingbird in Europe.
